items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “an increase in the proportion of a population living in urban areas”.
items.answer: Urbanisation
items.markingKey: Urbanisation: an increase in the proportion of a population living in urban areas. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between urbanisation and urban growth.
items.answer: Urbanisation is an increase in the proportion of people living in urban areas; urban growth is an increase in the urban population or area, which can occur without urbanisation if rural population grows as fast.

items.stem: Explain the causes of suburbanisation in HICs.
items.answer: Improved transport (railways, cars, roads); rising incomes; desire for space and gardens; cheaper land; planned housing estates; decline of inner-city environments.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per cause [4]

items.stem: Table 17.1 shows the percentage of the population living in urban areas in 1950 and 2020: UK: 79% to 84%; Brazil: 36% to 87%; China: 12% to 64%; Nigeria: 10% to 53%. Calculate the change in percentage points for each country.
items.answer: UK +5; Brazil +51; China +52; Nigeria +43

items.stem: Table 17.1 shows the percentage of the population living in urban areas in 1950 and 2020: Kenya: 6% to 29%; Ethiopia: 5% to 22%; UK: 79% to 84%; Mexico: 43% to 81%. (a) Calculate the change in percentage points for each country. (b) Explain why urbanisation is slowing in some countries.
items.answer: (a) Kenya +23; Ethiopia +17; UK +5; Mexico +38 (b) A high proportion is already urban; counter-urbanisation; fewer rural people left to migrate.

items.stem: Table 17.1 shows the percentage of the population living in urban areas in 1950 and 2020: Nigeria: 10% to 53%; Japan: 53% to 92%; Brazil: 36% to 87%; India: 17% to 35%. (a) Calculate how many times greater the urban share was in 2020 than in 1950 for each country. (b) Explain why urbanisation is slowing in some countries.
items.answer: (a) Nigeria 5.3 times; Japan 1.7 times; Brazil 2.4 times; India 2.1 times (b) A high proportion is already urban; counter-urbanisation; fewer rural people left to migrate.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that the cycle of urbanisation is equally applicable to cities in HICs and LICs.
items.answer: For: Many MIC cities show suburbanisation (Bangkok, São Paulo) and some re-urbanisation of centres; the sequence is visible in HIC cities such as London. Against: Most LIC cities are still in rapid urbanisation, driven by migration and natural increase; informal growth at the periphery is not suburbanisation in the HIC sense; counter-urbanisation is rare. Conclusion: The cycle describes HIC experience well but only partly fits LIC cities, which are at different stages and grow through different processes.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “urbanisation”?
options: The outward spread of urban areas as people, housing and services move to the edge of a city.
The movement of people back into city centres after a period of decline.
An increase in the number of people living in urban areas or in the area covered by towns.
An increase in the proportion of a population living in urban areas.
items.answer: An increase in the proportion of a population living in urban areas.
items.markingKey: Urbanisation: an increase in the proportion of a population living in urban areas. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “All countries pass through the cycle of urbanisation at the same time.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. HICs urbanised in the 19th-20th centuries; many LICs are urbanising rapidly now.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain the causes of re-urbanisation.
items.answer: Regeneration of inner cities and waterfronts; gentrification; new jobs in services; young professionals and students; government policies (brownfield targets); city-centre amenities.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per cause [3]

items.stem: Table 17.1 shows the percentage of the population living in urban areas in 1950 and 2020: Kenya: 6% to 29%; India: 17% to 35%; Bangladesh: 4% to 39%; China: 12% to 64%. Which country had the largest increase in percentage points?
items.answer: China
items.markingKey: Kenya +23; India +18; Bangladesh +35; China +52 [1]

items.stem: Table 17.1 shows the percentage of the population living in urban areas in 1950 and 2020: Kenya: 6% to 29%; UK: 79% to 84%; Japan: 53% to 92%; Nigeria: 10% to 53%. Explain why urbanisation is slowing in some countries.
items.answer: A high proportion is already urban; counter-urbanisation; fewer rural people left to migrate.

items.answer: (a) Kenya +23; Bangladesh +35; China +52; Brazil +51 (b) Kenya 4.8 times; Bangladesh 9.8 times; China 5.3 times; Brazil 2.4 times

items.answer: (a) HICs were already highly urbanised in 1950 and changed little; MICs urbanised rapidly; LICs still have low levels but are urbanising fast. (b) A high proportion is already urban; counter-urbanisation; fewer rural people left to migrate.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point with data [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “an urban area with a population of more than 10 million”.
items.answer: Megacity
items.markingKey: Megacity: an urban area with a population of more than 10 million. [1]

items.stem: Explain why the number of megacities has increased.
items.answer: Rapid urbanisation in LICs and MICs through rural-urban migration and natural increase; concentration of investment and industry; globalisation; agglomeration of services.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per factor [3]

items.stem: Explain the characteristics that make a city a world city.
items.answer: Headquarters of TNCs and banks; stock exchanges; international airports and connectivity; cultural influence; international organisations; global media.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per characteristic [3]

items.stem: In India, the largest city, Delhi, has a population of about 33.8 million and the second city, Mumbai, about 21.7 million. Suggest one problem of high urban primacy for a country.
items.answer: Regional inequality, congestion and overloaded infrastructure in the primate city, neglect of other regions.

items.stem: In Kenya, the largest city, Nairobi, has a population of about 5.3 million and the second city, Mombasa, about 1.4 million. (a) Calculate the primacy index (largest ÷ second-largest city). (b) Compare the actual population of the second city with the rank-size prediction.
items.answer: (a) 3.8 (b) Actual 1.4 million is smaller than the predicted 2.65 million, so the urban system is dominated by a primate city.

items.stem: Assess the view that the problems of megacities outweigh their benefits. In your answer you may refer to informal settlements and governance.
items.answer: For: Congestion, pollution (Delhi), informal housing (Mumbai’s Dharavi), water shortages, flooding (Jakarta), inequality. Against: Megacities generate a large share of national GDP, innovation and jobs; economies of scale make services cheaper per person; they offer opportunities to migrants; well-managed examples (Tokyo). Conclusion: Problems are severe in fast-growing LIC megacities, but benefits are large; the balance depends on governance and investment.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a city with major influence on the global economy through finance, trade, culture and decision-making, such as London, New York or Tokyo”.
items.answer: World (global) city
items.markingKey: World (global) city: a city with major influence on the global economy through finance, trade, culture and decision-making, such as London, New York or Tokyo. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “All megacities are world cities.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Some megacities such as Dhaka or Kinshasa have large populations but little global economic influence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain the problems faced by megacities in LICs.
items.answer: Informal settlements; inadequate water, sanitation and waste disposal; traffic congestion and air pollution; unemployment and informal work; crime; flood and hazard risk.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per problem [4]

items.stem: Table 17.2 shows the populations (millions, about 2023) of five megacities: Tokyo 37.1, Dhaka 23.9, Mexico City 22.5, Mumbai 21.7, Lagos 16.5. Suggest why population figures for megacities vary between sources.
items.answer: Different definitions of the boundary (city proper, urban agglomeration, metropolitan region); informal settlements undercounted; census dates differ.

items.stem: In India, the largest city, Delhi, has a population of about 33.8 million and the second city, Mumbai, about 21.7 million. (a) Compare the actual population of the second city with the rank-size prediction. (b) Suggest one problem of high urban primacy for a country.
items.answer: (a) Actual 21.7 million is larger than the predicted 16.9 million, so the urban system is more balanced (binary or polycentric). (b) Regional inequality, congestion and overloaded infrastructure in the primate city, neglect of other regions.

items.stem: In Peru, the largest city, Lima, has a population of about 11.3 million and the second city, Arequipa, about 1.1 million. (a) Compare the actual population of the second city with the rank-size prediction. (b) Suggest one problem of high urban primacy for a country.
items.answer: (a) Actual 1.1 million is smaller than the predicted 5.65 million, so the urban system is dominated by a primate city. (b) Regional inequality, congestion and overloaded infrastructure in the primate city, neglect of other regions.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “an area of unplanned housing built without legal permission, often lacking basic services”.
items.answer: Informal settlement
items.markingKey: Informal settlement: an area of unplanned housing built without legal permission, often lacking basic services. [1]

items.stem: Explain why informal settlements develop in LIC cities.
items.answer: Rapid in-migration and natural increase; shortage of affordable formal housing; low incomes; land on steep slopes, floodplains or near railways is vacant; lack of planning control.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per factor [4]

items.stem: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of the informal sector.
items.answer: Advantages: provides jobs and incomes, cheap goods and services, flexible, uses skills. Disadvantages: low and irregular pay, no rights or security, no tax revenue, unsafe conditions, child labour.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [4]

items.stem: Briefly describe living conditions in the settlement, for Favela-Bairro, Rio de Janeiro or another example of an informal settlement.
items.answer: Favela-Bairro, Rio de Janeiro: About 1 in 5 Rio residents lived in favelas such as Rocinha on steep hillsides; landslide risk; crime and drug gangs; few services.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Housing, services, employment, density, with figures. [5]

items.stem: Briefly describe living conditions in the settlement, for Dharavi, Mumbai or another example of an informal settlement.
items.answer: Dharavi, Mumbai: About 1 million people in about 2.1 km²; dense housing; shared toilets (one for hundreds of people in places); but about 5000 businesses and 15 000 single-room factories (recycling, pottery, leather) with an output of several hundred million US dollars a year.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Housing, services, employment, density, with figures. [5]

items.stem: Referring to Favela-Bairro, Rio de Janeiro or another example of an informal settlement, assess how successful attempts to improve living conditions in informal settlements have been.
items.answer: Model answer (Favela-Bairro, Rio de Janeiro): About 1 in 5 Rio residents lived in favelas such as Rocinha on steep hillsides; landslide risk; crime and drug gangs; few services. Favela-Bairro (1994-2008) upgraded around 150 favelas with paved roads, water, sanitation, crèches and some land titles; later Morar Carioca and police pacification units; improved services but gang violence persists.

items.stem: A student writes: “Informal settlements are always places of despair.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Many are vibrant communities with businesses, social networks and gradual improvement (e.g. Dharavi’s recycling industry).
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why slum upgrading is often preferred to demolition.
items.answer: It keeps communities and livelihoods intact, is cheaper, uses residents’ labour, and avoids moving people far from work; e.g. Favela-Bairro in Rio, Kampung Improvement in Indonesia.

items.stem: A survey of 60 households in a favela in São Paulo found the number of households with: piped water inside the home: 38; a private toilet: 26; electricity: 20; a member working in the informal sector: 38; a member who migrated from a rural area: 27. Suggest a suitable method of presenting these results.
items.answer: A bar chart (percentages for each service), as the categories are not parts of one whole, so a pie chart is unsuitable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark method; 1 mark justification [2]

items.stem: A survey of 80 households in an informal settlement in Manila found the number of households with: piped water inside the home: 5; a private toilet: 11; electricity: 10; a member working in the informal sector: 19; a member who migrated from a rural area: 60. (a) Suggest a suitable method of presenting these results. (b) Explain how the lack of services could affect residents’ health and livelihoods.
items.answer: (a) A bar chart (percentages for each service), as the categories are not parts of one whole, so a pie chart is unsuitable. (b) Lack of clean water and sanitation spreads diarrhoeal disease and cholera; time spent collecting water; illness reduces earnings; women and girls most affected.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark method; 1 mark justification [2] (b) [3]

items.stem: Assess the view that self-help and upgrading schemes are the most effective way of improving informal settlements. In your answer you may refer to hazardous sites and cost.
items.answer: For: Upgrading is cheaper, keeps communities and livelihoods, and uses residents’ skills (Favela-Bairro, Kampung Improvement Programme, Orangi Pilot Project in Karachi). Against: Upgrading may not reach the poorest or tenants; densities remain high; some sites are hazardous and need relocation; large-scale public housing (Singapore, China) has rehoused millions. Conclusion: Upgrading with secure tenure is usually most effective, but must be combined with new affordable housing and relocation from hazardous sites.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “informal settlement”?
options: A scheme in which authorities provide plots with basic services such as water and sanitation, and residents build their own homes.
An area of unplanned housing built without legal permission, often lacking basic services.
A scheme in which residents build or improve their own homes with materials, land or loans provided by authorities.
Economic activity that is not taxed, registered or regulated by the government.
items.answer: An area of unplanned housing built without legal permission, often lacking basic services.
items.markingKey: Informal settlement: an area of unplanned housing built without legal permission, often lacking basic services. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “The informal sector can make up the majority of urban employment in LICs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. In many sub-Saharan African cities over 70% of jobs are informal.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A revision website states: “Forced eviction is the most effective solution to informal settlements.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the advantages and disadvantages of the informal sector.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. It destroys homes and livelihoods without addressing the housing shortage; upgrading is generally more effective. (b) Advantages: provides jobs and incomes, cheap goods and services, flexible, uses skills. Disadvantages: low and irregular pay, no rights or security, no tax revenue, unsafe conditions, child labour.

items.stem: Name a case study of an informal settlement you have studied. For your example, evaluate the attempts to improve the settlement.
items.answer: Dharavi, Mumbai: Redevelopment plans since 2004 propose high-rise rehousing with free flats for eligible residents (Adani group project from 2022); critics fear loss of businesses and ineligible residents; NGOs support sanitation and community toilets.

items.stem: A survey of 100 households in an informal settlement in Manila found the number of households with: piped water inside the home: 37; a private toilet: 75; electricity: 17; a member working in the informal sector: 88; a member who migrated from a rural area: 28. items.answer: (a) piped water inside the home 37%; a private toilet 75%; electricity 17%; a member working in the informal sector 88%; a member who migrated from a rural area 28% (b) A bar chart (percentages for each service), as the categories are not parts of one whole, so a pie chart is unsuitable.

items.stem: Using a named example of an informal settlement you have studied, assess how successful attempts to improve living conditions in informal settlements have been.
items.answer: Model answer (Favela-Bairro, Rio de Janeiro): About 1 in 5 Rio residents lived in favelas such as Rocinha on steep hillsides; landslide risk; crime and drug gangs; few services. Favela-Bairro (1994-2008) upgraded around 150 favelas with paved roads, water, sanitation, crèches and some land titles; later Morar Carioca and police pacification units; improved services but gang violence persists.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the outward spread of urban areas as people, housing and services move to the edge of a city”.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A revision website states: “Counter-urbanisation and re-urbanisation can happen at the same time.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the causes of re-urbanisation.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Different groups move in different directions, e.g. families leave while young professionals move into city centres. (b) Regeneration of inner cities and waterfronts; gentrification; new jobs in services; young professionals and students; government policies (brownfield targets); city-centre amenities.

items.stem: “The cycle of urbanisation is equally applicable to cities in HICs and LICs.” How far do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: Many MIC cities show suburbanisation (Bangkok, São Paulo) and some re-urbanisation of centres; the sequence is visible in HIC cities such as London. Against: Most LIC cities are still in rapid urbanisation, driven by migration and natural increase; informal growth at the periphery is not suburbanisation in the HIC sense; counter-urbanisation is rare. Conclusion: The cycle describes HIC experience well but only partly fits LIC cities, which are at different stages and grow through different processes.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Primate cities can concentrate investment at the expense of other regions.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “All megacities are world cities.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Bangkok and Lima dominate their national economies, widening regional inequality. (b) Not correct. Some megacities such as Dhaka or Kinshasa have large populations but little global economic influence.

items.answer: (a) Correct. Bangkok and Lima dominate their national economies, widening regional inequality. (b) Rapid urbanisation in LICs and MICs through rural-urban migration and natural increase; concentration of investment and industry; globalisation; agglomeration of services.

items.stem: Table 17.2 shows the populations (millions, about 2023) of five megacities: Dhaka 23.9, São Paulo 22.8, Cairo 22.6, Mumbai 21.7, Lagos 16.5. Suggest why population figures for megacities vary between sources.
items.answer: Different definitions of the boundary (city proper, urban agglomeration, metropolitan region); informal settlements undercounted; census dates differ.

items.stem: In Brazil, the largest city, São Paulo, has a population of about 22.8 million and the second city, Rio de Janeiro, about 13.8 million. (a) Using the rank-size rule, calculate the expected population of the second city. (b) Suggest one problem of high urban primacy for a country.
items.answer: (a) 11.4 million (b) Regional inequality, congestion and overloaded infrastructure in the primate city, neglect of other regions.

items.stem: Jonas argues that the problems of megacities outweigh their benefits. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to governance, economic output and informal settlements.
items.answer: For: Congestion, pollution (Delhi), informal housing (Mumbai’s Dharavi), water shortages, flooding (Jakarta), inequality. Against: Megacities generate a large share of national GDP, innovation and jobs; economies of scale make services cheaper per person; they offer opportunities to migrants; well-managed examples (Tokyo). Conclusion: Problems are severe in fast-growing LIC megacities, but benefits are large; the balance depends on governance and investment.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “informal sector”?
options: Improving existing informal settlements by adding services, paving and secure tenure rather than demolishing them.
A scheme in which authorities provide plots with basic services such as water and sanitation, and residents build their own homes.
Economic activity that is not taxed, registered or regulated by the government.
A scheme in which residents build or improve their own homes with materials, land or loans provided by authorities.
items.answer: Economic activity that is not taxed, registered or regulated by the government.
items.markingKey: Informal sector: economic activity that is not taxed, registered or regulated by the government. [1]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Forced eviction is the most effective solution to informal settlements.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.

items.stem: A survey of 50 households in a favela in São Paulo found the number of households with: piped water inside the home: 10; a private toilet: 26; electricity: 16; a member working in the informal sector: 47; a member who migrated from a rural area: 30. (a) Suggest how the households could be sampled to make the results representative. (b) Explain how the lack of services could affect residents’ health and livelihoods.
items.answer: (a) Systematic sampling of every nth dwelling along transects, or stratified sampling by zone of the settlement; random starting point; avoid only main paths. (b) Lack of clean water and sanitation spreads diarrhoeal disease and cholera; time spent collecting water; illness reduces earnings; women and girls most affected.

items.stem: Assess the view that self-help and upgrading schemes are the most effective way of improving informal settlements. In your answer you may refer to tenure and cost.
items.answer: For: Upgrading is cheaper, keeps communities and livelihoods, and uses residents’ skills (Favela-Bairro, Kampung Improvement Programme, Orangi Pilot Project in Karachi). Against: Upgrading may not reach the poorest or tenants; densities remain high; some sites are hazardous and need relocation; large-scale public housing (Singapore, China) has rehoused millions. Conclusion: Upgrading with secure tenure is usually most effective, but must be combined with new affordable housing and relocation from hazardous sites.
